Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock trades at 153.2 times its earnings over the past twelve months, compared with 23.0 for the S&P 500. Buyers paying that price appear to be betting on sustained expansion. During an August 3 call, management pointed to a single customer segment outpacing the rest of the business and raised its 2026 forecast for that group. Who are those customers, and how much are they already buying?

Palantir's American Business Customers Are Buying Fastest

Those customers are American companies. Palantir generated $764 million in U.S. commercial revenue during the second quarter of fiscal 2026, a 149% increase from a year earlier. Sales to the U.S. government, the company's other major domestic market, grew 90% over the same period, meaning domestic corporate sales are expanding faster than sales to the government.

The client roster is expanding alongside those sales, though at a slower pace. Palantir finished the quarter with 653 U.S. commercial customers. That total is up 35% from a year earlier, suggesting individual clients are spending more on average.

Newly signed contracts reflect a similar trend. U.S. commercial bookings, which track the total value of agreements signed during the quarter, climbed 153% from a year earlier to a record $2.132 billion. That figure is almost three times the U.S. commercial revenue generated over the same three months. However, bookings count the full value of contracts, and management noted that some of these deals extend for three years.

How Big Could Palantir's Sales To American Companies Get?

Management expects U.S. commercial revenue to exceed $3.424 billion in 2026, representing growth of at least 134%. That target would account for about 42% of the $8.15 billion to $8.158 billion in total revenue the company forecast for the year. While both figures are projections rather than reported results, they demonstrate that sales to American companies have evolved past being a side business for Palantir.

The share price appears to assume a good deal of that growth already. Palantir trades at 75.1 times its sales over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 trades at 3.1 times. The stock delivered a 54.6% return from July 22 to October 20, 2026, compared with 3.1% for the index. On October 20, shares closed 7.9% below their highest close of the past year.

Fed rate hikes stock sectors performance chart. Photo by BeInCrypto

Citi's Tyler Radke says AI is creating software winners and losers. He expects Microsoft's revenue growth to top 20% while Adobe feels pressure as AI projects absorb corporate budgets.

Radke, Citi's co-head of US software equity research, told Bloomberg Television the sector looked very different earlier this year. At that point, a chip stock at the bottom of its sector still beat software's top performer.

Who Are the Software Winners and Losers as AI Reshapes Budgets?

In the Bloomberg interview, Radke said AI is lifting growth at Microsoft, Palantir, and Snowflake, a cloud data company.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ubSzSCDBgGg

In contrast, Adobe and smaller application vendors face pressure as information technology (IT) budgets shift to AI, he said.

Microsoft anchors his case, with Office priced under $100 a month and bundling security and Copilot, its AI assistant.

Meanwhile, he says rivals charge hundreds of dollars monthly, which leaves Microsoft room to monetize further.

For context, Microsoft's revenue grew 18% in the quarter ended June 30.

Radke added that Citi's survey of chief information officers (CIOs) places Microsoft's in-house AI models near the leading labs.

Is Consolidation the Next Phase for Pressured Software Makers?

Salesforce offered a fresh example on Tuesday. A filing shows it agreed to buy Braze, a customer engagement platform, for $47.50 per share in cash.

Salesforce shares rose about 20% after its last quarterly report, Radke noted.

Even so, he says, the question after half a dozen large deals is whether Salesforce can speed up organic growth.

Moreover, higher financing costs could add to that pressure. Citi's neocloud debt thesis blames bond yields, not weak demand, for the selloff in AI cloud providers.

In addition, Radke said 2026 capacity at those providers is sold out, making a total AI bust hard to picture.

He expects scale to decide who survives, with larger providers likely to outlast smaller rivals if capital stays costly.

Katie Stockton, founder of research firm Fairlead Strategies, lists wider credit spreads among three stock warning signs.

If financing stays costly, the split Radke describes could widen, as strategic buyers and private equity firms target pressured makers.

title: Mural, a startup founded by former Palantir engineers, raises $15 million bid to connect banks to the emerging bot economy
detail:
Mural, a startup founded by former Palantir engineers, raises $15 million bid to connect banks to the emerging bot economy
Chris Fernandes (left) and Sinclair Toffa (right) founded Mural to help businesses manage payments across currencies and borders. · Fortune · COURTESY OF MURAL
Camila Grigera Naón
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 7:00 AM MST 3 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The stablecoin boom has promised to make global commerce faster and cheaper by easing cross-border money transfers. But delivering on that promise remains complicated, as businesses still have to juggle banks, payment providers, and a patchwork of regulations. New York-based startup Mural wants to fix that problem by offering businesses one place to manage international payments, rather than having to piece together the system themselves. 

Cofounded by former Palantir engineers Sinclair Toffa and Chris Fernandes in 2022, Mural announced Tuesday that it has raised a $15 million Series A funding round. The startup plans to use the funds to further build out its platform, which allows customers—including payroll providers, software companies and fintechs—to rely on a single account that can hold traditional dollars, local currencies, and stablecoins.

"[We are] building this… compliant system of record that allows for businesses and fintechs to launch new financial products on top of us," Toffa, who serves as Mural's CEO, explained.

Fintech innovation has reshaped how money moves in recent years, and stablecoins have become part of that shift. These cryptocurrencies, typically designed to track the U.S. dollar, can move across borders in seconds, sometimes only for pennies in network fees. Stablecoin payments reached roughly $400 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up from the same period a year earlier, per a report from global consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. Their use for international transfers has also grown: cross-border stablecoin flows totaled $220 billion from July 2025 through June 2026, up nearly 78% from the previous 12 months, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.

Tether, the issuer behind the USDT stablecoin, led Mural's Series A, with participation from North Island Ventures. The round brings Mural's total funding to $28 million, following a $5 million seed round in 2022 and additional pre-seed and interim financing from earlier backers. Mural declined to disclose its valuation following its latest fundraising round. 

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said the investment also reflects a bet on AI agents becoming regular handlers of financial services.

"Those agents will need access to payment systems that operate around the clock and can reach people across the world," he told Fortune in a written statement. 

From Palantir to payments

Toffa's interest in international payments began when he visited Togo, his grandfather's home country, when he was 15 years old. His relatives there, who routinely received remittances from his father in the United States, told him that transfers could take weeks to arrive and cost as much as 20% in fees.

Key Takeaways

Palantir shares rose 4% today after Knox Systems announced a partnership to bring commercial software into FedRAMP and IL5 federal environments.

The deal lets other companies' software reach the government through Palantir's federal accreditations, which makes Palantir more central to how agencies get new technology.

No financial terms were disclosed, and analysts already expect revenue to climb from $4.48 billion in 2025 to $8.22 billion in 2026.

The next test is the third-quarter report, which management guided to $2.16 billion to $2.164 billion of revenue.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) shares are up 4% today after Knox Systems announced a partnership, before Monday's open, to get commercial software into the government's most tightly secured clouds.

That wins back part of Friday's 7% drop, which pushed the stock into a correction. (Tech is having a good day, too: the QQQ QQQ:NASDAQ is up nearly 2%.)

What exactly happened

Knox, which is private, runs a managed federal cloud and says it can get software makers FedRAMP authorization in 90 days or less. It already hosts more than 100 AI and enterprise applications, for customers including Adobe (ADBE:NASDAQ), Sierra and Armis.

Palantir has already helped software companies deploy to federal agencies on its own accredited infrastructure, IL5 environments included. Put the two together, and a software maker gets one route from authorization to deployment.

As Knox CEO Irina Denisenko said in the press release: "Knox exists to get the best software in the world to the government faster, and to protect it once it's there."

Neither company disclosed financial terms.

Palantir becomes the on-ramp

Those accreditations are the hard part for any software maker selling to the Pentagon, and this deal puts Palantir's to work for other companies' products.

It also lands on top of a government business that's already flying. Palantir's U.S. government revenue rose 90% year over year to $809 million in Q2 2026, out of $1.94 billion in total revenue.

Analysts expect revenue to nearly double again this year, to $8.22 billion, and to reach $17.9 billion by 2028…

The multiple already came down
